what_it_does: Some AI models are 'dynamic' — they take shortcuts on easy inputs and do more work on hard ones, in principle saving a lot of computation. In practice, GPUs and specialized AI chips are designed around fixed, predictable workloads, so when computation amounts vary unpredictably at runtime, the hardware sits idle or wastes resources, erasing the theoretical savings. Adyna is a system that handles this by preparing several pre-compiled versions of each computation (called 'kernels' — self-contained GPU programs), each tuned for a different expected level of activity (e.g., 'about 30% of inputs are active' versus '80%'). At runtime, it measures the actual activity level and picks the best-matching pre-compiled version, ensuring the hardware is always running code matched to current conditions. An intelligent sampling algorithm limits how many pre-compiled versions must be stored, so on-chip memory is not overwhelmed, while still covering the realistic range of activity levels well.
